Who would contribute: Anthropologists and archaeologists; Population geneticists; Community historians. A student could start with: Which routes could people have taken into this region, and when were they open? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Flood stories, origin myths, and dream imagery that may hold memories of changing landscapes. Who would contribute: Folklorists; Psychologists of dreams and memory. A living library that gathers what people have recorded about parrots (scientific papers, veterinary case reports, avicultural journals, photographs, theses, citizen-science observations) and connects it while keeping every record's source and context. Founded and directed by EV Voltura, PhD (Texas A&M). Its work includes knowledge graphs, a history of parrot names since 1758, multilingual species names, a student-built cockatoo diet dataset, and a hyperspectral feather library. A participating node of The Open Commons of Learning.
Parrots, cockatoos, lories and their relatives, in the wild and in human care.
Proposed co-hub. Physics, chemistry and statistics.
Proposed side hub. Texas, South Dakota, Wisconsin and the Southwest read on the ground.
Avicultural bulletins, old books and records digitized and cataloged, because what gets preserved shapes the history future generations can read.
What parrots eat in the wild and in human care, recorded with the context needed to compare like with like.
Research that lets birds choose whether to take part, honesty about the costs of AI tools, and a future where humans and parrots coexist.
Hyperspectral imaging of feathers, including ultraviolet colors birds can see and people cannot.
Graphs that show where research is thick and where it is thin: maps of what has been published, not summaries of what is true. AI may help find links, reviewed by people.
hubs.t: Knowledge Graphs as Maps of the Literature

Scientific names change; historical names are part of the record, not mistakes. A translation table between old literature and current checklists, keeping each authority's decision.
Every record keeps its citation and context: wild or captive, where, when, and how it was reported. Conflicting reports stay visible, and evidence is weighed by how it was obtained.
Researchers, veterinarians, aviculturists, caregivers, students and enthusiasts are all teachers here. Student research, volunteers, citizen science, and a norm of kindness.
